## Diagnosing Cold Start Misfires on a Tuned MINI Cooper S

When you are dealing with an engine that misfires across all cylinders only during open-loop operation, the diagnostic path narrows significantly once you rule out the obvious mechanical failures. In your specific case with the 2008 JCW package, you have already eliminated ignition components (coils and wires) by virtue of their location on top of the plugs, addressed airflow restrictions via the intake manifold gasket and cracked pipe replacement, and verified the MAF sensor is reading correctly after cleaning. The fact that the issue vanishes once the engine warms up and enters closed-loop mode provides a crucial data point: the fuel delivery system is functioning correctly under steady-state conditions, but something is going wrong during the initial startup transient where the ECU relies on pre-programmed maps rather than real-time oxygen feedback.

The symptom of gray smoke combined with a "random" misfire code that later resolves to specific cylinders (2 and 4) strongly suggests an over-fueling event. During open loop, the Engine Control Unit (ECU) calculates fuel injector pulse width based on load, RPM, and throttle position. If the resulting air-fuel ratio is too rich, unburned hydrocarbons exit the exhaust, creating that gray smoke. The misfire occurs because there isn't enough oxygen to support combustion; the mixture simply won't ignite properly.

Your observation of Long-Term Fuel Trim (LTFT) fluctuating between -2.5% and 0% is consistent with a healthy system compensating for minor variances, but it doesn't tell the whole story during that first cold start window. LTFT averages data over thousands of miles, so a temporary rich condition at startup won't necessarily skew the long-term average immediately. What you need to look for in your USB scan tool is the **Short-Term Fuel Trim (STFT)** specifically during the first 60 seconds after cranking, and more importantly, the individual cylinder fuel trims if your scanner supports it. On many OBD-II compliant scanners, you can view "Fuel Trim" graphs that show real-time adjustments. If the STFT spikes positive significantly (e.g., +15% to +20%) immediately after startup before dropping back down as the system warms and switches to closed loop, this confirms the ECU is actively trying to lean out a mixture it perceives as rich, or conversely, that the mixture is so rich the sensor cannot react properly.

Given the JCW chip tune and larger exhaust, you are likely running a modified fuel map. Aftermarket tunes often prioritize aggressive throttle response by enriching the mixture at part-throttle loads. However, if the tune lacks proper "cold enrichment" logic or if the base fuel table is too aggressive for your specific ambient conditions, the ECU may be stuck in a loop where it injects too much fuel before the O2 sensor can tell it to pull back.

Another potential culprit often overlooked in tuned vehicles is the Idle Air Control (IAC) valve. If the IAC valve is sticking or leaking slightly more air than designed when cold, the ECU might interpret this as a lean condition and inject excessive fuel to compensate, leading to a rich misfire until the thermal expansion of the valve clears the stickiness. While you mentioned the LTFT was near zero last week, check the live data stream again; if the STFT is high during idle, the IAC is likely the bottleneck preventing the engine from maintaining a stable idle speed under load.

Before resorting to an expensive shop visit for compression testing (which would only confirm mechanical health you've already assumed), focus your scanning efforts on the fuel trim history specifically tagged as "Cold Start" or "Open Loop." If the data shows extreme positive trims during that window, the issue is almost certainly a software mapping error in your current tune rather than a hardware failure. You may need to flash a revised map with adjusted cold-start fuel tables or check if the tuner has updated their calibration for newer emission standards which might have altered how the ECU handles transition states.

If you are comfortable with command-line diagnostics, some advanced scanners allow you to export raw data logs to CSV files. Analyzing these logs offline can reveal patterns that a dashboard readout misses. Look for the correlation between throttle position commands and injector pulse width during the first minute of operation. If the pulse width remains constant while RPM fluctuates or if it spikes disproportionately high compared to stock maps, you have found your smoking gun.

In many cases similar to yours, the solution involves re-flashing a tune that accounts for the specific interplay between the larger intake and the modified exhaust flow during cold conditions. The "random" nature of the misfire code is often just how the ECU reports it when multiple cylinders are affected simultaneously by a global fueling error rather than an individual cylinder failure.
